extracted.intended_audience: Readers of The Spectator / educated early‑18th‑century English readers interested in manners, marriage, and moral satire
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for composing/commenting on social‑moral topics in the style of The Spectator: short, didactic, anecdote‑driven essays that judge conduct (marriage, greatness, vanity, insults) with ironic or moralizing tone. Emphasises concrete examples and classical allusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for a good husband or wife
rubrics_metrics.description: Discretion, virtue, good‑nature, and evenness of temper are necessary qualifications for the domestick character of husband or wife.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text states: "Discretion seems absolutely necessary... Virtue is the next necessary Qualification... Good-Nature is a third necessary Ingredient... Good-Nature is insufficient, unless it be steady and uniform, and accompanied with an Evenness of Temper." Examples and authority: Homer’s Penelope and Ulysses (fidelity), Brutus and Porcia (virtue and affection), Cæsar (humanity), Socrates and Marcus Aurelius (composed minds surviving difficult spouses). Practical advice: couples should habituate themselves during the first year to bear one another's faults; nuptial rites recommended mutual sweetness and complacency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage may produce love (love after marriage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Love can follow matrimony — marriage sometimes produces the affection that ordinarily leads to marriage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from correspondent's remark on Mrs. Fanny Fickle: "as Love generally produces Matrimony, so it often happens that Matrimony produces Love." Presented as a corrective to expectations that love must precede a happy marriage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flitch of Bacon — claimant eligibility and formal oath/process
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim the Bacon Flitch a married person must, after a Year and a Day of marriage, come in person to Whichenovre-Hall, bring two neighbours, and make a sworn declaration (oath) before the steward and witnesses that since marriage he "would not have chaunged for none other; farer ne fowler; richer, ne pourer..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process details preserved in the Register: claimant must be received by bailiff/porter, assigned a day, bring two neighbours who swear to his marital status and freedom, the claimant kneels, places his hand on a Book laid upon the Bacon and Corn, and makes the oath. If declared a free‑man by neighbours, he receives half a quarter of wheat and a cheese (if a villain, half quarter of rye without cheese). By‑laws add that the wife shall take the same oath (mutatis mutandis) and judges may interrogate/cross‑examine witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flitch of Bacon — concrete disqualifying behaviors and evidentiary examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific faults or incidents recorded in the Register disqualified claimants: bribery/falsely swearing, domestic disputes about the bacon, hesitation at oath words, prior sexual/romantic misconduct misrepresented, displays of ambition, scolding, domineering speech, petty jealousies, public quarrels, spoiled dinners, coming home late, excessive fondness for pets, usurping household roles (e.g. poker/coalfire), tearing bills, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous anecdotal depositions are given as grounds for rejection: Aubry de Falstaff bribed witnesses and lost the bacon; Alison boxed her husband’s ear; Philip de Waverland "stole off" the oath clause; Richard de Loveless hesitated and tried to count pre‑marriage affection as compliance; Joceline Jolly got only a rasher for one month’s affection; examples of being rejected include the wife who said "God forgive him," the wife who declared "it was her Duty to obey" (interpreted oddly), a lady enamoured of her lap‑dog, a woman who turned away a house‑maid, quarrels over tavern or tailor bills, spoiling dinners, late arrivals, scolding about overboiled eggs, usurping the poker ("so far usuped the Dominion of the Coalfire"). These serve both as evidentiary behaviours and as telling comic negatives for marital felicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity of external trappings as a mark of affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: External ornaments (e.g. large scarfs worn by young divines/chaplains) are signs of vanity or affectation and should be exposed as an extravagance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letter-writer criticises town clergy and chaplains who wear large scarfs to appear Doctors; notes nobility’s privilege of creating chaplains leads to many nominal holders with adornments but little substance. Use of this point as satirical target: expose petty displays that imitate rank or learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: True greatness is measured by private virtue, not pomp or titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness is not conferred by wealth, titles, or public pomp but by contempt for those shows and by private acts of benevolence, humility, justice, and constancy; obscure private virtue may be superior to public fame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit moral thesis: "Nothing... can be Great, the Contempt of which is Great." Examples and imagery: angels would rank a philosopher in a cottage above a victorious general; private actions listed as glorious: contemplation, voluntary acts of justice to one's own detriment, concern for others, silent tears, subdued resentments, humility. Classical examples: Virgil’s Aglaës (happier gardener) contrasted with Gyges (rich king), Cowley’s poem quoted to illustrate preferring private peace to public glory. Advice for readers: do not be led by censure or applause; evaluate by what will stand when "Wisdom shall be justified of her Children."

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct concerning insults, exposure, and cowardice
rubrics_metrics.description: It is cowardly to insult someone who cannot avenge themselves; equally cowardly to passively forbear resenting an affront when resistance would not risk life; exposing or boasting of a woman's supposed favours is infamous; a generous person’s resentment dies when the other is powerless or in misfortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Lesbia’s letter and the editorial response: the writer condemns a man who publicly boasts of seduction or exposes a woman’s past, urging such conduct be made as infamous as taking a lie or not resenting a slap. Moral distinction: "It is a Mark of Cowardice passively to forbear resenting an Affront, the Resenting of which would lead a Man into Danger; it is no less a Sign of Cowardice to affront a Creature, that hath not Power to avenge it self." A story of violent revenge (Spanish lady) is offered as a deterrent and moral exemplum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for ancestry should be earned, not demanded
rubrics_metrics.description: Paying respect to worthy ancestors is laudable, but descendants should receive honour, not demand it by reminding others of their lineage; boasting of ancestors invites disadvantageous comparison and shows folly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: pedigrees often hide tradesmen and rustics; tracing a family backward reveals varied fortunes—claiming constant high birth is misleading. Satirical recommendation: do not claim a title to respect solely by descent; true merit comes from present conduct, not ancient ancestors.
